Columbus, Ohio Design-Build Home Remodeling — Kitchen, Bath, Basement & More

Design-build kitchen, bathroom, basement and whole-home remodeling for Columbus, Ohio homeowners.

Request a Consultation
(614) 562-0172

WHAT WE DO

Columbus Home Remodeling - From Kitchen Refreshes to Whole Home Renovations

Every Elevate project is led by the same small team — design through final walkthrough. 

Kitchen Remodeling

Layouts, custom cabinetry, stone, lighting, and millwork — designed for how your family actually lives.

Whether you're opening up a closed-off galley or refreshing the finishes in a colonial, we handle the full scope from design through final walkthrough. Our cabinetry is custom-built by Amish craftsmen right here in Ohio, and every project includes 3D renderings so you can see the finished kitchen before we start demo. From countertop selection and lighting design to appliance planning and finish carpentry, it's all coordinated under one roof.

KITCHEN REMODELING IN COLUMBUS, OHIO →

Whole Home Renovation

Modernize a historic home or reimagine a newer build. We coordinate every trade so you don't have to.

A whole-home remodel brings everything together — kitchen, baths, living spaces, flooring, trim, and finishes — into one cohesive design. Instead of tackling rooms one at a time with different contractors, you get a single team managing the full project from concept to completion. We help you figure out which walls can move, where storage should go, and how to make the flow of your home match how you actually live in it. 

WHOLE HOME REMODELING IN COLUMBUS, OHIO →

Spa-inspired primary baths, functional hall baths, and elegant powder rooms — with thoughtful tile, plumbing, and lighting choices throughout.

We design bathrooms that hold up to daily life and still feel like a retreat. Walk-in showers with frameless glass and custom tile work, heated floors, freestanding tubs, built-in storage that keeps countertops clean — it's all planned in detail before construction starts. Whether it's a full primary suite overhaul or a tub-to-shower conversion, every project is waterproofed, permitted, and built to last.

Bathroom Remodeling

BATHROOM REMODELING IN COLUMBUS, OHIO →

Basement Finishing

Custom basement finishing designed for entertaining, everyday living, and added home value.

A finished basement adds real, usable square footage to your home — whether that's a family room, home office, guest suite, gym, or all of the above. We handle the full build from framing and electrical to flooring, trim, and a full bathroom if you need one. That includes cutting and trenching the slab for plumbing, managing moisture with proper waterproofing and ventilation, and designing a layout that feels like a natural extension of the rest of your house. Thoughtful layouts, premium materials, and clear communication from start to finish.

BASEMENT REMODELING & FINISHING IN COLUMBUS, OHIO →

Recent kitchens & baths in Central Ohio.

SELECT PROJECTS

Kitchens, baths, and whole-home work from across greater Columbus — every photo is a real Elevate project.

WHY E L E V A T E

One Team. Design through Final Walkthrough. 

Most remodeling companies hand your project off to a different crew at every stage — one person sells it, someone else designs it, and a rotating cast of subs builds it. At Elevate, you work with the same small team from your first conversation through the day we hand you the keys.

Michael Freed, the owner, is personally involved in every project. He's been in the remodeling industry since 2012 and has hands-on construction experience — he understands what's behind your walls, what a realistic timeline looks like, and how to solve problems before they become expensive surprises. That field knowledge is baked into every design decision, material recommendation, and budget conversation.

Here's what that means in practice: you get 3D renderings before we start demo so there are no surprises. You get a dedicated point of contact who actually knows the status of your project. You get Amish-crafted custom cabinetry built to order in Ohio — not pulled from a catalog. And you get honest communication about budget, timeline, and scope from the very first meeting.

We're licensed and insured in the State of Ohio, and we carry a 4.9-star rating on Google with consistent five-star reviews.

This is your home. You deserve a remodeling experience that respects your time, your investment, and your trust.

Trusted by Columbus Homeowners

We carry a 4.9-star rating on Google — and every review comes from a real homeowner we've worked with across Central Ohio. 

C O N T A C T   U S

Beautiful renovations begin with a conversation.

Speak directly with our design-build team and get honest guidance on your project — no pressure, no obligation.

Elevate Remodeling

Elevate Remodeling is a Columbus, Ohio design-build remodeling company. We specialize in kitchen remodeling in Columbus, bathroom remodeling in Columbus, basement finishing and whole home remodels. Neighborhoods we serve: Upper Arlington, Dublin, Powell, Bexley, Grandview Heights, Clintonville, Worthington, Westerville, New Albany, Hilliard, Gahanna, Lewis Center, Delaware, Galena, Plain City and surrounding neighborhoods. Most of the bathrooms we remodel were built between the 1920s and the 1970s, and the era tells you a lot about what we'll find behind the walls.

Pre-war homes in Clintonville, Bexley, and Old Arlington usually have plaster over wood lath, cast iron waste lines, and a single small bathroom that was generous by 1928 standards. Galvanized supply lines are common and typically need replacing as part of the scope.

Homes built in the 1990s and later in Dublin, Powell, and Lewis Center usually have the square footage but builder-grade finishes and awkward layouts — oversized garden tubs nobody uses, cramped shower stalls, and vanities that waste the wall.

We scope for what these homes usually hide and build contingencies into the estimate, so a surprise inside a wall doesn't turn into a surprise on your invoice.

Whole Home Renovations in Columbus, Ohio

A whole-home renovation brings multiple rooms and systems under one cohesive plan — rather than remodeling your kitchen this year, your bathrooms next year, and your living spaces the year after that. We design and build the entire scope as a single, coordinated project so finishes flow from room to room, trades work efficiently, and you only live through one construction timeline.

This is interior renovation of your existing home — not an addition. We work within your current footprint to reimagine layouts, update every surface and system, and create a home that looks and functions the way you need it to. Whether you're modernizing a 1960s ranch in Upper Arlington or gutting a colonial in Worthington, the scope is tailored to your home and your priorities.

Every whole-home project follows our standard design-build process: consultation, scope and proposal, design with 3D renderings, curated selections and signoff, production, and final walkthrough. Why Upper Arlington Homes Need a Different Approach 

Upper Arlington homes have great bones. The neighborhoods are established, the architecture has character, and the lots are generous. But most of these homes were designed 50 to 80 years ago — before open-concept kitchens, spa bathrooms, and flexible living spaces became the standard.

At Elevate Remodeling, we work with Upper Arlington homeowners to bring those homes up to how families actually live today. Our kitchen and bathroom remodels and renovations are designed to feel like they belong in the house — not like an addition bolted on. We handle everything from design and material selection through permitting and construction, with one team and one point of contact throughout. 

Kitchen & Bathroom Remodeling for Upper Arlington, Ohio Homeowners
Opening Closed Floor Plans

Many Upper Arlington homes were designed with separated kitchens and compartmentalized layouts. We help homeowners create more connected living spaces through thoughtful reconfiguration and structural planning.

Expanding Kitchen Functionality

Older kitchens often lack storage, workspace, and flow. Custom cabinetry, integrated storage, and improved layouts can dramatically enhance functionality while preserving the home’s character. 

Updating Primary Bathrooms

We frequently help homeowners transform outdated bathrooms into bright, functional retreats with larger showers, custom vanities and timeless material selections.

Preserving Architectural Character 

Thoughtful remodeling should feel cohesive with the original home. We carefully balance modern functionality with architectural details that complement the existing space. 

Kitchen Remodeling in Upper Arlington

Upper Arlington kitchen remodeling starts with understanding what older homes do well — and where they fall short. Closed floor plans separate the cook from the rest of the family. Cabinets stop short of the ceiling. Counter space runs out. And the whole room feels dark despite windows that should be doing more work.

 Our kitchen remodeling in Upper Arlington projects typically address all of this — and more.

 We start by looking at the structure. Many UA kitchens can be opened to the dining room or living space by removing a non-load-bearing wall, or in some cases with a beam and post solution when structural support is needed. The result is a connected living space where the kitchen is part of the room, not separated from it.

 From there, we focus on the details that have the most impact on daily use: cabinet layout and storage, countertop material and workspace, lighting (task, ambient, and accent), and appliance placement. We work with custom and semi-custom cabinetry, quartz and natural stone countertops, and a full range of finishes, following the same design-build approach behind all of our kitchen remodeling in Columbus.

 A few things that come up often on Upper Arlington kitchen remodels:

Opening the kitchen to the living or dining area for a more connected layout

Adding an island or peninsula where there wasn't one before

Colonial Revivals throughout the neighborhood often have more formal layouts — separate dining rooms, closed-off living spaces, and kitchens that were designed for a time when cooking happened out of sight. Dublin homes range from established neighborhoods with traditional architecture to newer master-planned communities with contemporary designs — but homeowners across the city often share similar goals: more functional kitchens, updated bathrooms, and living spaces that reflect how their families actually live today.

Understanding Dublin Homes

Dublin is one of the largest and most geographically diverse suburban cities in Central Ohio, and that diversity shows up directly in the remodeling work we do there. Unlike Bexley or Grandview Heights — where the housing stock is relatively uniform in age and style — Dublin spans several distinct eras of development and several very different homeowner profiles. Understanding which part of Dublin a home is in tells you a lot about what the remodel will involve.

The oldest established areas of Dublin — the neighborhoods surrounding Historic Dublin Village, along High Street and the streets near the Scioto River — contain homes built from the 1960s through the 1980s. These are ranch homes, split-levels, and two-story traditionals that have been in families for decades. They have good bones, established landscaping, and mature lots, but kitchens and bathrooms that haven't been meaningfully updated since they were built. Remodeling in these neighborhoods often involves reconfiguring layouts that were designed for a different era — opening up walls between the kitchen and living space, replacing single vanities with double, adding storage where there isn't any. The work is familiar but requires careful attention to the home's original structure.

Moving further out, the large master-planned communities that define much of Dublin's growth from the late 1980s through the 2000s — neighborhoods like Muirfield Village, Ballantrae, Tartan Fields, and the communities surrounding the Dublin Athletic Club — tell a different story. These homes were built with more square footage, more formal layouts, and higher-end exterior finishes than the typical Columbus suburb. But interiors from that era have aged in consistent ways: builder-standard cabinetry, early-generation granite or Corian countertops, Jacuzzi tubs as the primary bathroom statement piece, and kitchens that were spacious but designed around a more formal, separated approach to entertaining. The remodeling here is less about reconfiguration and more about a material and design refresh — replacing what's there with something custom, cohesive, and current.

Dublin's newer developments, particularly around the Bridge Park mixed-use district and the communities continuing to grow along I-270's northwest corridor, represent a third profile entirely. These homes are newer, often more contemporary in design, and come with better standard finishes than older production builds — but homeowners in these neighborhoods are often ready to personalize spaces that still feel generic. Custom cabinetry, statement lighting, and material upgrades that reflect the homeowner's actual taste rather than a builder's defaults are the most common starting point.

Basement renovations in Dublin are among the most common projects we take on. These spaces are frequently under-finished relative to the rest of the house. Large footprints with high ceilings that are being used for storage rather than living. Given Dublin's family-oriented demographic, finished basements here commonly become rec rooms, home theaters, kids' homework areas, or full guest suites. The ceiling heights in most Dublin basements (typically 8 to 9 feet) make these genuinely versatile spaces when designed well.

Dublin kitchens from the 1990s and 2000s share a consistent set of limitations — not because the homes were built poorly, but because production builders optimized for square footage and layout over materials and detail. The result is kitchens that are spacious by Columbus standards, often with islands and open adjacency to the family room, but finished with stock cabinetry, laminate or early-generation granite, and lighting that was never really designed at all.

The transformation we make most often in Dublin is replacing that production-built feel with something genuinely custom — and the difference is significant. Better cabinetry construction with full-extension drawers and interior details that actually function. Natural stone or quartz that was selected for the specific space rather than pulled from a builder's allowance list. A range hood that anchors the room instead of blending into the ceiling. Lighting designed in layers — task, ambient, and accent — so the kitchen works at 7am and at a dinner party. It's how we approach kitchen remodeling in Columbus on every project, regardless of scope.

We recently completed a full kitchen remodel in Bellepoint Place that's a good example of what this looks like in practice. The bones were solid — good square footage, island already in place, open to the living area. What changed was everything you see and touch: custom cabinetry to the ceiling, quartz countertops, integrated appliances, statement lighting, and a range wall that became the focal point of the main floor.

 A few things that come up consistently on Dublin kitchen remodels:

Replacing builder-standard cabinets with custom or semi-custom cabinetry built to the ceiling

Upgrading countertops from early-generation granite or laminate to natural stone or quartz

Adding a statement range hood and upgrading to chef-grade appliances with proper ventilation

Adding a butler's pantry or expanded storage where the layout allows

And the whole room feels dated despite being technically functional.

The most common primary bath project we do in Dublin is repurposing that tub footprint into a larger walk-in shower — typically curbless, with frameless glass, quality tile work, and a rain head or multi-function system that actually justifies the space. The square footage is already there. It just needs to be used differently. See how we handled exactly that in a recent Bellepoint Place bathroom remodel.

Beyond the shower, Dublin primary bath remodels typically include a double vanity with real storage, updated plumbing and lighting fixtures, heated floors, and a material palette — tile, stone, hardware — that feels cohesive and considered rather than builder-standard. The goal is a bathroom that functions like a private retreat and holds up to daily use without looking like it was finished from an allowance list. It's the same process our Columbus bathroom remodelers follow on every project, in Dublin and across Central Ohio.

Understanding Grandview Heights Homes

Grandview Heights is a small city — just under 2 square miles — and almost every inch of it is residential. The housing stock was built primarily between the 1910s and the 1950s, with Craftsman bungalows, American Foursquares, Cape Cods, and modest Colonial Revivals making up the majority of homes along streets like Roxbury Road, Broadview Avenue, and the avenues running off of Grandview Avenue itself. These are well-built, well-loved homes. They're also consistently smaller than what most buyers are used to finding in the Columbus suburbs, and that constraint shapes almost every remodeling conversation we have in this neighborhood.

The average Grandview home runs somewhere between 1,000 and 1,800 square feet. That's not a lot of room to work with — which means every square foot matters, and every design decision carries more weight than it would in a larger home.

Kitchen Remodeling in Grandview Heights

Kitchens in Grandview homes are almost universally compact and separated from the main living area. In a Craftsman bungalow that usually means a galley tucked toward the back of the house, with minimal counter space, limited cabinet storage, and a layout that made sense when cooking was a solitary activity. Most of these homes were built in the 1920s and 30s, and the original kitchen was never meant to be a place anyone gathered.

The most transformative thing we can do in many of these homes is open the wall between the kitchen and the dining room. That takes a careful structural assessment — older framing behaves differently than new construction, and what's load-bearing isn't always obvious. When it works, a closed galley becomes part of a connected living space and the whole main floor feels different.

When that isn't structurally feasible, the focus shifts to making the existing footprint work as hard as it can: custom cabinetry built to the ceiling, integrated appliances, a layout that eliminates wasted steps, and lighting that makes the room read larger than it measures. Finishes are chosen to complement the home's original character rather than fight it. It's the same approach we take on every project regardless of size as kitchen remodeling contractors in Columbus.

A few things that come up often on Grandview kitchen remodels:

Opening the wall between the kitchen and dining room where the framing allows

Custom cabinetry built to the ceiling to recover vertical storage

Counter-depth or integrated appliances that don't eat floor space

Relocating the sink or range to cut wasted steps in a galley layout

Layered and under-cabinet lighting to make a small room read larger

Finish selections that complement original hardwood and trim

Timelines and costs vary depending on scope — a cosmetic refresh looks very different from a full layout change. If you're in the early planning stages, our 2026 Columbus kitchen remodel cost guide breaks down typical price ranges by project tier, so you can get a realistic sense of budget before your first consultation.

Most homes have one or two bathrooms shared by the whole household, built for a smaller family and a different era of daily life. That reality pushes the design conversation toward efficiency and impact. A walk-in shower in place of a tub that rarely gets used. A vanity with actual drawer storage instead of a pedestal sink. Large-format tile on the floor and walls to visually expand the room. A lighting plan that makes the space feel considerably larger than its square footage suggests. In some homes there's also room to add. We've carved second baths out of underused space — an oversized closet, a wide landing, a corner of a bedroom that wasn't doing much. It takes planning around existing plumbing runs and it isn't possible everywhere, but when it is, it changes how the whole house functions. Small-footprint work is some of the most demanding work we do as bathroom remodeling contractors in Columbus. 

What we handle on Grandview bathroom remodels: 

Tub-to-shower conversions in 5x7 and 5x8 footprints

 Custom vanities with real drawer storage, sized to the space 

Large-format tile on floor and walls to visually expand the room 

Carving out a second bath from an underused closet or landing

Recessed and vanity lighting planned for rooms with little natural light 

Pocket doors and wall-mounted fixtures where every inch counts

Understanding Clintonville Homes

South Clintonville — roughly everything south of North Broadway — is the oldest part of the neighborhood. Homes here were built primarily before 1930, many originally developed as streetcar communities. The architecture runs from Craftsman bungalows and American Foursquares to Sears kit homes, Tudor Revivals, and Dutch Colonials. These homes tend to sit on narrow lots with alley access, and feature original hardwood floors, built-in cabinetry, decorative woodwork, and front porches that define the streetscape. The kitchens and bathrooms are often small and largely original — full of charm but in need of thoughtful updating.

North Clintonville, stretching from North Broadway to the Overbrook Ravine, represents the neighborhood's next wave of growth from the 1920s through the late 1950s. Homes here were built as higher-end properties for the era, and they reflect the increasing role of the automobile — driveways replaced alley access, and lots grew slightly larger. Architectural styles range from late Tudors and Colonials to early midcentury ranches and Cape Cods. Many of these homes have more space to work with than their southern neighbors, but their kitchens and bathrooms are often just as dated.

Beechwold, at the northern end of Clintonville, contains the widest variety of housing in the neighborhood — from modest Cape Cod starter homes to sprawling custom builds on wooded lots. Named for the Jeffrey family's summer estate, Beechwold has a slightly more suburban feel than the rest of Clintonville while maintaining the mature trees, walkability, and neighborhood identity that draws people to the area. Homes here range from the 1930s through the 1960s, and many are ready for interior updates that match the quality of the lots and locations they sit on.

Basements across Clintonville reflect the same range as the houses above them. Pre-war homes in the south end typically have ceilings under seven feet, original block or stone walls, and mechanicals that were never placed with finished space in mind. Beechwold and the later North Clintonville builds often have more height to work with. We scope every one around what's actually there — ceiling height, moisture, and egress first — which is how we approach finished basements across Columbus generally.

About Clintonville, Ohio

Clintonville is one of Columbus's oldest and most distinctive neighborhoods — a seven-square-mile community just north of Ohio State University that has been drawing residents since the early 1900s, when downtown residents and OSU professors began building summer homes along its wooded ravines. Over the following decades, the neighborhood filled in with streetcar-era housing, midcentury development, and the kind of mature landscaping that only comes with a hundred years of growth. Today, Clintonville is home to roughly 30,000 residents and consistently ranks among the most sought-after neighborhoods in the city.

What sets Clintonville apart is its walkability and independent identity. North High Street runs through the center of the neighborhood as a thriving commercial corridor lined with locally owned restaurants, cafes, breweries, and shops — from Katzinger's and Brassica to Clintonville Outfitters and the Wexner Center satellite gallery. The neighborhood's six glacial ravines carve through the landscape and create a park system that feels surprisingly natural for an urban community, with Whetstone Park, the Park of Roses, and Overbrook Ravine among the most popular green spaces.

Clintonville is served by Columbus City Schools, with Clinton Elementary and Indianola Informal K-8 among the most popular neighborhood schools. Families, young professionals, OSU faculty, and long-time residents all share the same sidewalks here — which is part of what gives the neighborhood its unusually strong sense of community. Annual events like the Clintonville Farmers' Market and the Fourth of July parade are fixtures, not afterthoughts.

For homeowners, Clintonville offers something rare in the Columbus market: genuine architectural character, walkable access to daily needs, and proximity to both downtown and the university — all in a neighborhood where people invest in staying rather than moving on. That makes remodeling here a natural decision and a smart long-term investment.
